stem: You want a README to appear at the top of your GitHub profile page, where your username is `mira-dev`. What does GitHub require?

options.text: A `PROFILE.md` file in any repository, pinned to the top of your profile
options.why: GitHub looks for `README.md` in one specially named repository, not a file in any pinned repo.

options.text: A public repository named `mira-dev` with a non-empty `README.md` at its root
options.why: Those are the three conditions GitHub checks before showing a profile README.

options.text: A private repository named `.github` containing a `profile/README.md` file
options.why: A `.github/profile/README.md` is the organization profile pattern, and it is not for personal accounts.

options.text: Text typed into the Bio field in your profile settings, which supports full Markdown
options.why: The bio is a short plain field; the rich profile README comes from a repository.

explanation: GitHub shows a profile README when a public repository has the same name as your username and contains a non-empty `README.md` in its root. Making the repository private, or emptying or deleting the file, removes it from the profile.
reference: GitHub Docs: Managing your profile README

stem: A secret gist is private: only you and the people you explicitly invite can view it.

options.text: True
options.why: Secret gists are not access-controlled, so this statement does not hold.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: secret only means unlisted. Anyone who has the URL can open a secret gist.

explanation: Secret gists do not appear in Discover and are not searchable by others, but they are not private: anyone with the URL can view them. Never put credentials in a gist of either kind; GitHub even scans secret gists for partner secrets because they leak.
reference: GitHub Docs: Creating gists

stem: Match each organization repository role with the access it is designed for.

options.text: Read
Triage
Write
Maintain
Admin

prompts.text: A non-code contributor who views code and opens issues and discussions
A contributor who labels, assigns and closes issues and pull requests without push access
A developer who pushes branches and merges pull requests
A project manager who manages the repository without sensitive or destructive actions
Someone who needs full access, including security settings and deleting the repository

explanation: Repository roles in an organization go Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, Admin. Triage exists so people can manage issues and pull requests without write access, and Maintain covers repository management short of sensitive or destructive actions, which stay with Admin.
reference: GitHub Docs: Repository roles for an organization

stem: The organization `acme` enables GitHub Pages on its repository named `handbook`. With no custom domain, at which URL is the site served?

options.text: `https://handbook.github.io/acme`
options.why: The owner name comes first in the hostname, not the repository name.

options.text: `https://github.com/acme/handbook/pages`
options.why: Pages sites are served from the `github.io` domain, not from github.com paths.

options.text: `https://acme.github.io/handbook`
options.why: A project site is served from the owner domain with the repository name as the path.

options.text: `https://acme.github.io`
options.why: That root URL belongs to the organization site, which must live in a repository named `acme.github.io`.

explanation: There are two kinds of Pages site. A user or organization site must be in a repository named `<owner>.github.io` and is served at `https://<owner>.github.io`. Any other repository publishes a project site at `https://<owner>.github.io/<repository>`.
reference: GitHub Docs: About GitHub Pages

stem: When a webhook has a secret configured, GitHub sends an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the payload in a request header. Type the name of that header.
explanation: The `X-Hub-Signature-256` header carries `sha256=` followed by the hex HMAC-SHA256 digest of the payload, keyed with your webhook secret. The older `X-Hub-Signature` header uses HMAC-SHA1 and exists only for legacy reasons. If no secret is configured, the header is not sent.
reference: GitHub Docs: Validating webhook deliveries

stem: A research group wants visitors to their repository to get a ready-made citation for the software in formats such as APA and BibTeX. What should they add?

options.text: A `CITATION` section in `README.md`, which GitHub parses automatically
options.why: GitHub does not parse README prose into citation formats.

options.text: A `CITATION.cff` file at the repository root on the default branch
options.why: GitHub reads it and adds a "Cite this repository" link to the sidebar.

options.text: A release with the DOI typed into the release title
options.why: Releases do not generate citation prompts from their titles.

options.text: A `codemeta.json` file in the `.github` folder of the organization
options.why: GitHub does not build its citation prompt from this file in the `.github` folder.

explanation: `CITATION.cff` is the Citation File Format, plain YAML that is both human- and machine-readable. When it is on the default branch, GitHub adds a "Cite this repository" link that offers formatted citations such as APA and BibTeX.
reference: GitHub Docs: About CITATION files

stem: Users keep opening issues that are really open-ended questions, such as "Which database do you recommend with this library?", cluttering the bug tracker. Which GitHub feature is designed for this?

options.text: GitHub Discussions, for example a Q&A category where an answer can be marked
options.why: Discussions suit open conversation; issues are for trackable work.

options.text: A wiki page, because any user can edit it to add their own questions and answers
options.why: Wikis are documentation, not a threaded place to ask and answer questions.

options.text: Gists, because each question can live in its own small repository
options.why: Gists share snippets; they are not a community forum for a project.

options.text: GitHub Projects, adding each question as a draft item on a board
options.why: Projects plan and track work; they do not host conversations.

explanation: Issues are for actionable, trackable work such as bugs and tasks. Discussions give a project a forum for questions, ideas and announcements, and a Q&A category lets maintainers mark the accepted answer. An issue can also be converted into a discussion when it turns out to be a question.
reference: GitHub Docs: About discussions

stem: Which statements about GitHub Releases are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each release is based on a Git tag that marks a point in history
options.why: Releases are built on tags; creating a release can create the tag too.

options.text: GitHub attaches zip and tarball archives of the source at that tag
options.why: These source archives are added automatically to every release.

options.text: Binary assets must be committed to the repository before they can be attached
options.why: Assets are uploaded to the release itself, not committed to Git.

options.text: Release notes must always be written by hand in the release form
options.why: GitHub can generate release notes automatically from merged pull requests.

options.text: A repository can only ever have one release, which is replaced each time
options.why: A repository can have many releases, one per tag.

explanation: Releases package a tagged point in history. GitHub adds zip and tarball source archives automatically, and you can upload binaries as release assets without committing them. Release notes can be generated automatically and customised with `.github/release.yml`.
reference: GitHub Docs: About releases

stem: A team wants pull requests that keep every npm dependency on its latest version every week, whether or not a vulnerability has been reported. Which feature do they configure?

options.text: Dependabot alerts, which open an update pull request for each outdated package
options.why: Alerts notify you about vulnerable dependencies; they do not open routine update PRs.

options.text: Dependabot security updates, which bump packages to their newest release
options.why: Security updates only target dependencies with an alert, and move to the minimum patched version.

options.text: Dependabot version updates, scheduled in a `.github/dependabot.yml` file
options.why: Version updates raise PRs for outdated dependencies on the schedule you set.

options.text: Code scanning default setup, which flags outdated packages during CodeQL analysis
options.why: CodeQL analyses your own code for vulnerabilities, not dependency versions.

explanation: Dependabot has three parts. Alerts tell you a dependency is vulnerable. Security updates open PRs to move vulnerable dependencies to the minimum patched version. Version updates, configured in `.github/dependabot.yml`, keep dependencies current on a schedule regardless of vulnerabilities.
reference: GitHub Docs: About Dependabot version updates

stem: A developer runs `git push` with a commit that contains a live AWS access key. The organization wants the key never to reach the repository in the first place. Which feature does that?

options.text: Secret scanning alerts, which flag the key after it has been pushed
options.why: Alerts fire after the secret is already in the repository, which is too late here.

options.text: Secret scanning push protection, which rejects the push with an explanation
options.why: It blocks the push before the commit lands, unless someone bypasses with a reason.

options.text: Dependabot security updates, which strip credentials from commits
options.why: Dependabot manages dependencies; it never inspects commits for secrets.

options.text: Code scanning with CodeQL, which fails the pull request that adds the key to the code
options.why: CodeQL looks for vulnerable code patterns, and it runs after the push.

explanation: Push protection checks pushes for supported secrets and blocks them before they land. By default anyone with write access can bypass it by giving a reason, which is recorded in the audit log and may raise an alert; delegated bypass can restrict who is allowed to do that.
reference: GitHub Docs: About push protection

stem: An organization hires a contractor who needs write access to exactly one repository and must not become an organization member. How should they be added?

options.text: As an organization member, with that repository set as their only team
options.why: Members count as part of the organization and receive the base permission.

options.text: As a billing manager, which grants repository access without membership
options.why: Billing managers handle billing; the role gives no repository access.

options.text: By adding their SSH key as a deploy key with write access on the repository
options.why: Deploy keys are for machines and cannot be tied to a person.

options.text: As an outside collaborator on that repository with the Write role
options.why: Outside collaborators get access to specific repos without joining the org.

explanation: An outside collaborator is not an organization member but has access to one or more of its repositories. They do not receive the organization base permission and do not see other repositories, which fits contractors and partners.
reference: GitHub Docs: Adding outside collaborators to repositories in your organization

stem: In an organization, the team hierarchy is Engineering > Application Engineering > Identity. Engineering has Write access to the `auth-service` repository; the two child teams have no direct access. What access do members of Identity have?

options.text: None, because access granted to a parent team never flows downward
options.why: Nested teams are designed so that it does flow down.

options.text: Read only, because child teams always receive one role lower than their parent team
options.why: There is no automatic downgrade between levels of the hierarchy.

options.text: Write, because child teams inherit the access permissions of their parent
options.why: Inheritance applies through every level of the hierarchy.

options.text: Write, but only after an owner approves each child team separately
options.why: Inherited access needs no separate approval per child team.

explanation: Child teams inherit their parent team's repository access, so granting Engineering write access also gives it to Application Engineering and Identity. That is why the docs advise giving parent teams only access that is safe for everyone below them, and adding extra access lower down. Mentions also flow down: members of child teams are notified when the parent team is mentioned.
reference: GitHub Docs: About teams

stem: Put the steps of a correct webhook signature check in order.

options.text: Read the raw request body bytes before any JSON parsing
Compute an HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of those bytes using the webhook secret
Prefix the digest with `sha256=`
Compare it with the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header using a constant-time comparison
Only then parse the JSON and queue the event for processing

explanation: The signature covers the exact bytes GitHub sent, so you must hash the raw body, not a re-serialised object. The header value always starts with `sha256=`. Compare with a timing-safe function such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual` or `hmac.compare_digest`, never `==`, and reject the request before acting on it if the signatures differ.
reference: GitHub Docs: Validating webhook deliveries

stem: A script calls the GitHub REST API without any token and starts getting `403 rate limit exceeded` errors after about an hour of light polling. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Switch to the GraphQL API, which has no rate limit for anonymous clients
options.why: GraphQL requires authentication and has its own points-based limit.

options.text: Add a `User-Agent` header, which raises the anonymous limit to 5,000
options.why: A User-Agent is required, but it does not change the rate limit.

options.text: Authenticate the requests, raising the limit from 60 to 5,000 per hour
options.why: Unauthenticated calls share a small per-IP limit; authenticated ones get far more.

options.text: Spread the calls across more `per_page` values so each uses a fresh limit
options.why: The limit counts requests, not distinct URLs.

explanation: The primary REST rate limit for unauthenticated requests is 60 per hour, per originating IP address. Authenticated requests made as a user get 5,000 per hour. Making conditional requests with ETags also helps, because a `304 Not Modified` response does not count against the primary rate limit.
reference: GitHub Docs: Rate limits for the REST API

stem: A poller sends `If-None-Match` with the `etag` from its last REST response. Nothing has changed, so GitHub replies with a status code that does not count against the primary rate limit. Type that status code.
explanation: Conditional requests that return `304 Not Modified` don't use your primary rate limit, so polling with `If-None-Match` (or `If-Modified-Since`) is the recommended pattern. The saving only applies when the representation really is unchanged.
reference: GitHub Docs: Best practices for using the REST API

stem: You are reviewing pull request #482 and want its branch checked out locally to run the tests. Which GitHub CLI command does that in one step?

options.text: `gh repo clone 482`, which clones the pull request as a new repository
options.why: `gh repo clone` clones repositories, not pull requests.

options.text: `gh pr view 482 --web`, which downloads the branch while opening the browser
options.why: `--web` only opens the pull request in a browser.

options.text: `gh pr merge 482 --local`, which merges into a temporary local branch
options.why: There is no `--local` merge; `gh pr merge` merges on GitHub.

options.text: `gh pr checkout 482`, which fetches the PR branch and switches to it
options.why: It even handles branches that live in a contributor's fork.

explanation: `gh pr checkout <number>` fetches the pull request head, including from forks, and checks it out locally. Other everyday commands include `gh pr create --fill`, `gh pr merge --squash`, `gh release create v1.2.0 --generate-notes` and `gh api` for raw API calls.
reference: GitHub CLI manual: gh pr checkout

stem: On a personal account (not GitHub Enterprise Cloud), publishing a GitHub Pages site from a private repository keeps the site visible only to the repository's collaborators.

options.text: True
options.why: Private publishing is an Enterprise Cloud feature, so this statement does not hold.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the published site is public on the internet even though the repository is private.

explanation: Access control for Pages is only available to organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, where a project site can be published privately to people with read access. Otherwise a Pages site is public to anyone on the internet, even when its source repository is private, so never publish sensitive content there.
reference: GitHub Docs: Changing the visibility of your GitHub Pages site

stem: Match each GitHub product with what it is for.

options.text: GitHub Codespaces
GitHub Copilot
GitHub Sponsors
GitHub Marketplace
GitHub Classroom

prompts.text: A cloud development environment built from the repository's dev container configuration
An AI assistant that suggests code and answers questions in the editor and on GitHub
A way to fund the maintainers of open source projects you depend on
A catalogue of apps and actions that extend GitHub
A tool for teachers to distribute and collect coding assignments

explanation: Codespaces runs a dev container in the cloud, usually configured by `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`. Copilot is the AI assistant. Sponsors funds open source maintainers. Marketplace lists apps and actions. Classroom, part of GitHub Education, manages coursework through repositories.
reference: GitHub Docs: GitHub products

stem: Why does GitHub generally recommend a GitHub App over an OAuth app for a new integration? (Choose three.)

options.text: It requests fine-grained permissions instead of broad scopes
options.why: Permissions can be narrowed to exactly what the integration needs.

options.text: Whoever installs it chooses which repositories it can access
options.why: Repository selection at install time limits the blast radius.

options.text: Its installation access tokens are short-lived
options.why: Installation tokens expire after an hour, which limits damage if one leaks.

options.text: It always acts as the user who installed it, so audit logs show that person
options.why: A GitHub App can act on its own, as the app, without any user.

options.text: It can automatically access every repository the authorizing user can reach
options.why: That broad reach describes OAuth apps, and it is a drawback.

explanation: GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions, let installers pick repositories, and use short-lived tokens. They can act independently of a user, which suits automation, or on behalf of a user with a user access token. OAuth apps act only as the user and inherit everything that user can access within the granted scopes.
reference: GitHub Docs: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

stem: A docs site is built and deployed to GitHub Pages by a custom GitHub Actions workflow. To move it to `docs.example.com`, a teammate commits a `CNAME` file containing that domain to the repository root, but the site keeps serving on `github.io`. What is wrong?

options.text: The `CNAME` file has to sit in the `/docs` folder, not in the repository root
options.why: Its location in the repo is not the issue when an Actions workflow publishes the site.

options.text: Custom domains are only supported for sites built with Jekyll from a branch
options.why: Custom domains work with any publishing source, including Actions.

options.text: With Actions publishing, a `CNAME` file isn't used; set the domain in Pages settings
options.why: Only the settings page configures the domain for an Actions-published site.

options.text: The file must contain the full URL `https://docs.example.com/` rather than the domain
options.why: The domain alone is the right content; the scheme is not the problem.

explanation: When a site is published from a branch, saving a custom domain in the Pages settings commits a `CNAME` file to the source branch. When it is published by a custom GitHub Actions workflow, no `CNAME` file is created and one in the repository does nothing; you set the domain in the repository's Pages settings. You still need the DNS record pointing at GitHub.
reference: GitHub Docs: Managing a custom domain for your GitHub Pages site

stem: The user `octo` wants their user site (`octo.github.io`) to be served at `www.example.com`. Which DNS record should they create at their DNS provider?

options.text: An `A` record for `www.example.com` pointing to `github.com`'s IP address
options.why: Pages is not served from github.com addresses, and `A` records need IPs, not names.

options.text: A `CNAME` record for `www.example.com` pointing to `github.com/octo`
options.why: DNS records cannot point at URL paths, only at hostnames.

options.text: A `TXT` record for `www.example.com` containing `octo.github.io`
options.why: TXT records are used to verify a domain, not to route traffic.

options.text: A `CNAME` record for `www.example.com` pointing to `octo.github.io`
options.why: A subdomain points at the account's default Pages domain.

explanation: For a subdomain such as `www`, create a `CNAME` record that points to `<user>.github.io` (or `<org>.github.io`), without the repository name. An apex domain such as `example.com` instead uses `A` records for GitHub's Pages IP addresses (185.199.108.153 to 185.199.111.153) or an `ALIAS`/`ANAME` record. Then set the custom domain in the Pages settings.
reference: GitHub Docs: Managing a custom domain for your GitHub Pages site

stem: A company deletes the repository that hosted its Pages site, but its DNS still points `blog.example.com` at GitHub Pages. A week later the subdomain serves a stranger's content. What would have prevented this?

options.text: Verifying `example.com` for the account with a TXT record in DNS
options.why: Only repositories of the verifying account can then use the domain and its immediate subdomains.

options.text: Enforcing HTTPS on the site before the repository was deleted
options.why: HTTPS protects traffic in transit, not ownership of the domain.

options.text: Adding a wildcard `*.example.com` record pointing at GitHub Pages
options.why: Wildcard records make takeovers easier, and the docs warn against them.

options.text: Keeping the `CNAME` file in a fork of the deleted repository
options.why: A file in a fork does not reserve the domain for the company.

explanation: Leaving DNS pointed at GitHub after deleting the site lets another user claim the domain, which is a domain takeover. Verifying the domain with a TXT record means only repositories owned by the verifying account can publish to it and its immediate subdomains. Also remove stale DNS records and avoid wildcard records.
reference: GitHub Docs: Verifying your custom domain for GitHub Pages

stem: A webhook receiver processes each `push` event synchronously, running tests that take about 30 seconds before replying `200`. The deliveries page shows most deliveries as failed. Which two changes fix this properly? (Choose two.)

options.text: Respond with a 2xx right away and process the event later from a queue
options.why: GitHub fails deliveries that take longer than 10 seconds to answer.

options.text: Use the `X-GitHub-Delivery` ID to skip events you have already processed
options.why: Redeliveries reuse the same delivery ID, so it makes processing idempotent.

options.text: Raise the delivery timeout in the webhook settings to 60 seconds
options.why: The 10-second limit is fixed; there is no timeout setting to raise.

options.text: Rely on GitHub automatically retrying failed deliveries a few minutes later
options.why: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed webhook deliveries.

options.text: Switch to the `X-Hub-Signature` header so verification runs faster
options.why: The SHA-1 header is legacy; signature speed is not the bottleneck.

explanation: GitHub expects a 2xx response within 10 seconds and otherwise ends the connection and records a failure. Acknowledge quickly, push the work onto a queue, and make processing idempotent with `X-GitHub-Delivery`, which stays the same when a delivery is redelivered.
reference: GitHub Docs: Best practices for using webhooks

stem: Your webhook endpoint was down for two hours during a deploy. When it comes back, what happens to the deliveries that failed during the outage?

options.text: GitHub retries them with exponential backoff until your server responds
options.why: GitHub does not have an automatic retry schedule for webhooks.

options.text: GitHub queues them and delivers them in order once your endpoint answers again
options.why: There is no queue that drains when your server comes back.

options.text: Nothing, until you redeliver them yourself in the UI or via the API
options.why: Failed deliveries stay failed unless you redeliver them.

options.text: They are lost permanently and can only be reconstructed by polling events
options.why: Recent failed deliveries can still be found and redelivered.

explanation: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed webhook deliveries. Redeliver them manually from the deliveries page or write code that lists failed deliveries through the REST API and redelivers them. A redelivery keeps the same `X-GitHub-Delivery` header.
reference: GitHub Docs: Handling failed webhook deliveries

stem: A workflow in one repository uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` to call the REST API across many repositories in a large sweep and keeps hitting rate limits partway through. Which change raises the available rate limit most directly?

options.text: Add `sleep` calls between requests, because the `GITHUB_TOKEN` limit resets every minute
options.why: The limit is per hour, so short pauses only slow the sweep down.

options.text: Split the sweep into two workflows in the same repository, each with its own limit
options.why: The `GITHUB_TOKEN` limit is per repository, so both share it.

options.text: Add `permissions: write-all` so the token is given a higher limit
options.why: Permissions change what the token can do, not how many requests it gets.

options.text: Authenticate as a GitHub App installation with access to those repositories
options.why: Installation tokens get at least 5,000 requests per hour and can span many repositories.

explanation: The REST limit for `GITHUB_TOKEN` is 1,000 requests per hour per repository, and the token only covers its own repository by default. A GitHub App installation token has a minimum of 5,000 requests per hour (higher on Enterprise Cloud) and can be granted access to every repository the sweep needs. Conditional requests and fewer calls help too.
reference: GitHub Docs: Rate limits for the REST API

stem: A dashboard polls `GET /repos/acme/api/pulls` every minute with `If-None-Match`, but it never gets a `304` even when no pull requests changed. Each poll alternates between `per_page=30` and `per_page=50`. Why?

options.text: Pull request list endpoints never return an `etag` header
options.why: Most list endpoints return an `etag`, including this one.

options.text: A different page size is a different representation with its own `etag`
options.why: The saved `etag` only matches when the parameters are identical.

options.text: Conditional requests only work with the GraphQL API
options.why: Conditional `GET` requests are a REST feature.

options.text: The `etag` changes every minute because it is derived from the response `Date` header
options.why: Unrelated headers such as `Date` do not change the representation's `etag`.

explanation: A `304` is returned only when the representation matches the saved `etag`. Changing the page size, page number or filters produces a different response and a different `etag`, so always poll with the same parameters. Parameters such as `sort=updated` also reorder lists and invalidate pages more often.
reference: GitHub Docs: Best practices for using the REST API

stem: A developer creates one fine-grained personal access token and expects it to read repositories in both the `acme` and `globex` organizations. It only ever works for one of them. Why?

options.text: Fine-grained tokens can only read public repositories in any organization
options.why: They can access private repositories the owner and permissions allow.

options.text: Fine-grained tokens expire after one use per organization
options.why: Tokens are reused until they expire or are revoked.

options.text: Each fine-grained token is limited to a single resource owner
options.why: One token targets one user or organization, so they need one per organization.

options.text: Organizations must first convert the token into a classic token
options.why: Organizations can require approval, but they never convert token types.

explanation: When creating a fine-grained token you choose one resource owner, a user or an organization, and the token can only access that owner's resources. Organizations can also require approval before such tokens work. Classic tokens are broader but less controlled; a GitHub App is often the better fit for automation.
reference: GitHub Docs: Managing your personal access tokens

stem: An organization publishes a private container image to `ghcr.io/acme/base` from repository A. A workflow in repository B tries to pull it with `GITHUB_TOKEN` and gets `403 Forbidden`. What fixes this with the least privilege?

options.text: Make the image public so that every workflow in every repository can pull it without a token
options.why: That exposes the image to everyone instead of granting one repository access.

options.text: Store an owner's personal access token as a secret in repository B
options.why: A long-lived personal token grants far more than this pull needs.

options.text: Give repository B the `packages: admin` permission in its workflow file
options.why: A workflow cannot grant itself access to a package it was not allowed to use.

options.text: Grant repository B read access in the package's "Manage Actions access" settings
options.why: Container packages have granular permissions that allow specific repositories.

explanation: The Container registry supports granular permissions. By default `GITHUB_TOKEN` can work with packages associated with its own repository. To let a workflow in another repository pull the image, add that repository under the package's Actions access settings with read access.
reference: GitHub Docs: About permissions for GitHub Packages

stem: If you remove a person's access to a private repository, any forks they made of it on GitHub are deleted, but their local clones keep the code.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: their forks of that private repository are deleted, while local clones are untouched.

options.text: False
options.why: This statement does hold; it is the documented behaviour.

explanation: Removing someone's access to a private repository deletes their forks of it. GitHub cannot reach local clones, so they keep whatever they already pulled. Forks created in another organization are not deleted when individual access is removed. Treat code a person already cloned as disclosed.
reference: GitHub Docs: What happens to forks when a repository is deleted or changes visibility

stem: Match each GitHub security feature with what it does.

options.text: Dependabot alerts
Dependabot security updates
Code scanning (CodeQL)
Private vulnerability reporting

prompts.text: Notifies you that a dependency in your graph has a known vulnerability
Opens a pull request moving a vulnerable dependency to the minimum patched version
Analyses your own source code for vulnerabilities and coding errors
Lets a security researcher report a flaw to maintainers without making it public

explanation: Dependabot alerts and security updates deal with third-party dependencies; code scanning with CodeQL looks for problems in the code you wrote. Private vulnerability reporting gives researchers a confidential channel, after which maintainers can work in a draft security advisory and publish it when a fix is ready.
reference: GitHub Docs: GitHub security features

stem: A researcher finds a remote-code-execution bug in a popular public repository. The project has private vulnerability reporting enabled and a `SECURITY.md`. What is the responsible way to report it?

options.text: Open a public issue with a proof of concept so users can protect themselves
options.why: Public disclosure before a fix puts every user at risk.

options.text: Open a pull request with the fix so the vulnerability stays hidden
options.why: Fix pull requests in a public repository reveal the flaw to everyone.

options.text: Use "Report a vulnerability" in the Security tab, as SECURITY.md describes
options.why: This reaches the maintainers privately and starts a draft advisory.

options.text: Post it in GitHub Discussions so that maintainers can debate the severity
options.why: Discussions in a public repository are public too.

explanation: `SECURITY.md` describes how to report vulnerabilities, and private vulnerability reporting adds a "Report a vulnerability" form to the Security tab. Maintainers can then collaborate privately in a draft repository security advisory, prepare a fix and publish the advisory, optionally requesting a CVE.
reference: GitHub Docs: Privately reporting a security vulnerability

stem: What happens to forks when a repository's visibility changes? (Choose two.)

options.text: When a private repository is made public, its private forks stay private in separate networks
options.why: Forks keep their visibility and are split into their own networks.

options.text: When a public repository is made private, its public forks stay public in a separate network
options.why: Existing public forks are not made private or deleted.

options.text: When a private repository is made public, its private forks become public too
options.why: Forks are not flipped to public along with the upstream.

options.text: When a public repository is made private, its public forks are deleted
options.why: Public forks are detached, not deleted.

options.text: Forks always follow the upstream visibility, so nothing changes in practice
options.why: Visibility changes split forks off rather than changing them.

explanation: Visibility changes separate forks into new repository networks so fork owners can keep working. Private forks stay private when the upstream goes public, and public forks stay public when the upstream goes private. Deleting a private repository deletes its private forks.
reference: GitHub Docs: What happens to forks when a repository is deleted or changes visibility

stem: A GitHub App exchanges its JWT for an installation access token. After how many minutes does that installation access token expire? Type a number.
explanation: Installation access tokens expire after one hour, so long-running integrations must request a new one. Octokit SDKs regenerate them automatically. Short-lived tokens are one of the main security advantages GitHub Apps have over long-lived personal tokens.
reference: GitHub Docs: Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App

stem: An Express webhook handler uses `express.json()` and then checks `HMAC_SHA256(secret, JSON.stringify(req.body))` against `X-Hub-Signature-256`. Some deliveries pass, but many fail, especially ones with non-ASCII commit messages. What is the bug?

options.text: The handler should hash with SHA-1, because webhooks are signed with SHA-1
options.why: The `-256` header is HMAC-SHA256; SHA-1 is only the legacy header.

options.text: The secret must be base64-decoded before it is used as the HMAC key
options.why: The webhook secret is used as given, with no decoding step.

options.text: It hashes a re-serialised body instead of the raw bytes GitHub signed
options.why: Re-encoding changes whitespace and escaping, so the digest stops matching.

options.text: The comparison must be case-insensitive, because GitHub sends an uppercase digest
options.why: The digest is lowercase hex; casing is not the cause.

explanation: The signature is computed over the exact payload bytes. `JSON.stringify` of the parsed object can produce different whitespace or character escaping, so small ASCII payloads may happen to match while others fail. Capture the raw body (for example `express.raw()` or a `verify` hook) and hash that.
reference: GitHub Docs: Validating webhook deliveries

stem: A contributor pushes a commit containing a database password to their fork of a public repository, then deletes the fork an hour later. Is the secret still exposed?

options.text: No, because deleting the fork also deletes every Git object it pushed to the network
options.why: Deleting a fork does not purge Git data shared across the network.

options.text: Yes, because Git data in a network may stay reachable from other repos in it
options.why: Rotate the password; deleting the fork is not remediation.

options.text: No, as long as no one opened a pull request from the fork
options.why: Reachability does not depend on a pull request being opened.

options.text: Only if the upstream owner had already merged the commit
options.why: Unmerged commits can still be reachable through the network.

explanation: Repositories in a fork network share Git data, and GitHub states that data from any repository in a network may be accessible from any other repository in it, even after a fork is deleted. Treat any pushed secret as compromised: revoke and rotate it first, then clean up history.
reference: GitHub Docs: What happens to forks when a repository is deleted or changes visibility

stem: A developer pushed a live payment-provider API key to a public repository an hour ago. Which three actions belong in the response? (Choose three.)

options.text: Revoke the key with the provider and issue a new one right away
options.why: Rotation is the only step that stops further use of the leaked key.

options.text: Review the provider's logs for activity using the key since the push
options.why: You need to know whether the key was already abused.

options.text: Remove it from the code and enable push protection to prevent repeats
options.why: Cleanup plus prevention stops the same mistake happening again.

options.text: Make the repository private, which revokes access to the key everywhere
options.why: Anyone who saw or cloned it in that hour still has the key.

options.text: Force-push rewritten history, which on its own makes the key safe again
options.why: Rewriting history does not invalidate a key that is already public.

options.text: Delete the repository, because deletion removes the key from all caches
options.why: Forks, clones and caches may still contain it.

explanation: A secret pushed to a public repository must be treated as compromised, since scrapers find keys within minutes. Revoke and rotate it, check for misuse, then clean up and prevent recurrence with push protection. Making the repository private, rewriting history or deleting the repository do not make the old key safe.
reference: GitHub Docs: About push protection

stem: You are building a bot that comments on pull requests in 200 repositories of an organization, triggered by webhooks with no user signed in. Which design does GitHub recommend?

options.text: An OAuth app authorised by an admin, acting with that admin's token
options.why: Actions would appear as the admin and break if the admin leaves.

options.text: A classic personal access token from a bot user account with the `repo` scope
options.why: This means a long-lived, broadly scoped secret plus a seat for a fake user.

options.text: A deploy key on each repository, used to post comments over SSH
options.why: Deploy keys grant Git access, not API access to comment on pull requests.

options.text: A GitHub App installed on the org, using installation access tokens
options.why: The app acts as itself with fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens.

explanation: Automation that runs without a user should be a GitHub App acting as itself. The installer picks the repositories, permissions are fine-grained, and installation tokens last an hour. Comments are attributed to the app's bot identity rather than a person.
reference: GitHub Docs: Deciding when to build a GitHub App

stem: A GitHub App service needs to call the API as one of its installations. Put the authentication steps in order.

options.text: Sign a short-lived JWT with the app's private key
Call the endpoint that creates an installation access token for the installation ID
Use the returned installation token in API requests on that installation
Request a new installation token when the current one expires after an hour

explanation: An app first authenticates as itself with a JWT signed by its private key. That JWT is only good for app-level endpoints, such as creating an installation access token. The installation token is then used for the actual work and must be regenerated after it expires.
reference: GitHub Docs: Authenticating as a GitHub App installation

stem: A team publishes a Jekyll Pages site straight from a branch. During a busy release day they push to that branch dozens of times an hour, and later pushes stop updating the site promptly. What change avoids the problem?

options.text: Add a `.nojekyll` file so the branch build counts as a static upload
options.why: Branch publishing still runs a build for every push.

options.text: Build and publish with a custom GitHub Actions workflow instead
options.why: The soft limit of 10 builds per hour does not apply to custom workflows.

options.text: Move the site to a `/docs` folder, which has its own separate build quota
options.why: The folder choice does not change the build limit.

options.text: Enable Enterprise Cloud private publishing, which has no build limits
options.why: Private publishing controls access, not build quotas.

explanation: GitHub Pages has a soft limit of 10 builds per hour for branch-based builds; it does not apply when you build and publish with a custom GitHub Actions workflow. Other soft limits are a published site size of at most 1 GB and 100 GB of bandwidth per month.
reference: GitHub Docs: GitHub Pages limits

stem: An organization lowers its base permission for members from Write to Read. Several members have private forks of organization repositories. What happens to permissions on those private forks?

options.text: They are not updated automatically when base permissions change
options.why: Admins must review private fork permissions themselves.

options.text: They drop to Read immediately, matching the new organization base permission
options.why: The docs state private fork permissions are not updated automatically.

options.text: The private forks are deleted because their owners lost Write
options.why: Changing a base permission does not delete forks.

options.text: They become public forks in a separate network
options.why: Base permission changes never alter fork visibility.

explanation: Private forks inherit the upstream repository's permission structure when they are created, but changing the organization's base permissions does not automatically update permissions on existing private forks. Review them separately when tightening access.
reference: GitHub Docs: What happens to forks when a repository is deleted or changes visibility

stem: A GitHub App opens pull requests on behalf of the signed-in user using a user access token. The app has write access to `contents`, but the user only has Read on the target repository. What happens when the app tries to push a branch?

options.text: It succeeds, because the app's own permission level always wins
options.why: User access tokens are limited by the user's access as well.

options.text: It succeeds and is attributed to the app's bot account, not the user
options.why: User access tokens act as the user; they don't switch to the bot identity.

options.text: It fails, because a user access token only reaches what both can access
options.why: Access is the overlap of what the app and the user are allowed to do.

options.text: It fails, because GitHub Apps can never act on behalf of users
options.why: GitHub Apps can act for a user with a user access token.

explanation: When a GitHub App acts on behalf of a user, the user access token is limited both by the app's permissions and by the user's own access, so it can only do what both are allowed to do. To push without the user's permissions, the app would use an installation token and act as itself.
reference: GitHub Docs: Authenticating with a GitHub App on behalf of a user

stem: A reporting script sends one GraphQL query per hour that fetches 100 repositories, each with its last 100 pull requests and each pull request's last 50 comments. It burns through the hourly budget far faster than "one request" suggests. Why?

options.text: Each GraphQL request costs exactly one point, so other scripts must be sharing the budget
options.why: Cost is not a flat one point per request for large queries.

options.text: GraphQL queries count against the REST limit of 60 per hour
options.why: GraphQL has its own points-based limit; 60 per hour is the anonymous REST limit.

options.text: Nested connections are fetched with separate REST calls behind the scenes
options.why: GraphQL does not translate queries into REST calls.

options.text: Query cost depends on how many nodes the nested `first:` arguments could return
options.why: Large nested connections multiply into a much higher point cost.

explanation: The GraphQL API has a points-based primary limit (5,000 points per hour for users). A query's cost is calculated from the number of nodes its connections could return, so nested `first: 100` arguments multiply quickly. Request fewer nodes per level, paginate with cursors, or split the query.
reference: GitHub Docs: Rate limits and query limits for the GraphQL API

stem: A sync job lists all issues in a large repository through the REST API. Which two practices make the pagination correct and efficient? (Choose two.)

options.text: Follow the URL in the `Link` header's `rel="next"` instead of building page URLs
options.why: The `Link` header is the supported way to move between pages.

options.text: Use a stable sort order rather than `sort=updated` while paging
options.why: Sorting by updated time moves items between pages as they change.

options.text: Set `per_page=1000` so the whole list arrives in one response
options.why: List endpoints cap `per_page` at 100.

options.text: Assume a missing `Link` header means the request failed and retry
options.why: No `Link` header simply means everything fit on one page.

options.text: Fetch pages in parallel from page 1 to a guessed last page number
options.why: Guessing page numbers misses or duplicates items when data changes.

explanation: REST list endpoints paginate with a `Link` header containing `rel="next"`, `rel="last"` and so on; follow those links. Keep the sort stable while paging, because parameters such as `sort=updated` reorder the list as items change and shift items between pages you have already fetched.
reference: GitHub Docs: Using pagination in the REST API

stem: An organization switches on SAML single sign-on enforcement. The next morning, a developer's classic personal access token gets `403` on the organization's repositories but still works on their personal ones. What is the fix?

options.text: Regenerate the token with the `admin:org` scope added so it covers the organization
options.why: Extra scopes do not satisfy SSO enforcement.

options.text: Switch the remote URLs to SSH, which is exempt from SSO
options.why: SSH keys need SSO authorisation too under enforcement.

options.text: Authorise the token for the organization's SSO in token settings
options.why: Credentials must be authorised for the org once SSO is enforced.

options.text: Ask an owner to add the user as an outside collaborator
options.why: They are already a member; the token is what lacks authorisation.

explanation: Under SAML SSO enforcement, a personal access token or SSH key must be authorised for that organization before it can access the organization's resources. The token keeps working for resources outside the organization, which is why personal repositories still work.
reference: GitHub Docs: Authorizing a personal access token for use with single sign-on

stem: A repository offers several dev container configurations for Codespaces. Which file location is NOT detected as a selectable configuration?

options.text: `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`
options.why: This is the default configuration location.

options.text: `.devcontainer.json` in the repository root
options.why: A root-level file is supported if its name starts with a period.

options.text: `.devcontainer/database-dev/devcontainer.json`
options.why: Alternatives may live one subdirectory below `.devcontainer`.

options.text: `.devcontainer/team-a/testing/devcontainer.json`
options.why: Files more than one level below `.devcontainer` are not detected.

explanation: Codespaces looks for `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`, a root `.devcontainer.json`, and alternatives one directory level below `.devcontainer`. A file nested two levels down is ignored. Each codespace uses exactly one configuration, and settings are not inherited between configuration files.
reference: GitHub Docs: Introduction to dev containers
